desc: Selects everything from the active cell to the last used cell in the sheet — not the last cell with visible data, the last cell Excel has EVER touched, including old formatting on empty rows. Delete or format after this and you can affect far more than your actual data range.
Selects from the active cell back to A1 — same risk in reverse: a delete/format here touches everything above and to the left.
Extends the selection to the edge of the current data block in one jump — stops at the first blank cell, so a single gap in your data silently truncates the selection without any warning.

Inside a formatted Table, selects just the table data first; press again to select the whole sheet. Outside a table it selects the whole used range immediately — same shortcut, different blast radius depending on where your cursor is.
Shift+Space selects the entire row, Ctrl+Space selects the entire column of the active cell — instant full-row/column selection with no drag.
Selects the entire used range PLUS any embedded objects (charts, shapes, images) — a delete here removes visuals you didn't mean to touch.

Selects only the visible cells in a filtered range, excluding hidden/filtered-out rows. Without this, a normal selection on a filtered range silently includes the hidden rows too — meaning a paste or format change lands on rows you can't even see.
Toggles AutoFilter on/off for the current range instantly. In a shared/collaborative file, this changes what everyone sees when the file reopens — an accidental toggle looks like data went missing.
Opens the filter dropdown for the active column without touching the mouse.

Repeats your last action exactly — including a delete, a paste, a format change, or a formula fill. Pressing it out of habit on a different cell silently reapplies whatever destructive thing you just did.
Redo — reapplies the last undone action. Functionally the same trap as F4 in most contexts.
Excel's undo stack is deep (usually 100 steps) — most people give up after 2-3 presses and assume something is unrecoverable when it often isn't.

Forces a full recalculation of every formula in every open workbook, ignoring Excel's normal dependency-tracking shortcuts. On a large model with thousands of formulas this can freeze Excel for minutes — and it can also reveal (or mask) circular-reference and volatile-function bugs that a normal recalc wouldn't trigger.

Recalculates all open workbooks using the normal dependency tree. If a workbook is set to Manual calculation, this is the only thing that updates it — formulas can silently show stale values until you press this.
Recalculates only the active sheet, not the whole workbook — much faster on huge files, but easy to forget other sheets are now out of sync.

Toggles the entire sheet between showing values and showing the raw formula in every cell — the fastest way to audit a spreadsheet you didn't build, and also the fastest way to accidentally 'lose' your data view and panic.
Jumps directly to the cells a formula depends on (its precedents) — genuinely fast formula auditing most people do by eye instead.

Flash Fill: Excel infers a pattern from one example and rewrites an ENTIRE column to match it. Extremely powerful for reformatting data — and just as capable of silently overwriting a column of real data if your example row wasn't representative of every row below it.

cmd: Double-click fill handle   ·   Mac: Double-click fill handle
desc: Auto-extends a formula or series down to match the length of an adjacent filled column — convenient until that adjacent column has a gap or extends further than your actual data, silently overfilling.
Fills the selection down (D) or right (R) from the top/left cell — the keyboard-only version of dragging the fill handle, works on any size selection instantly.

Deletes the selected cells entirely and shifts the remaining cells to fill the gap — this is NOT the same as clearing content. Everything below/right physically moves up/left, which can misalign formulas referencing fixed positions elsewhere.
Inserts blank cells and shifts existing data to make room — the insert-side mirror of Ctrl+-, with the same risk of silently shifting rows out of alignment with formulas elsewhere in the sheet.
Clears cell CONTENT only — formatting, comments, and data validation stay. Looks like a full delete but isn't; use Ctrl+- if you actually want cells removed and everything shifted.

cmd: Ctrl+Shift+= (select row/col first)   ·   Mac: Cmd+Shift+= (select row/col first)
desc: With an entire row or column selected, inserts a whole new row/column and shifts everything else — a single accidental extra row inserted deep in a model can break every relative-reference formula built on top of it.
Switches between sheet tabs without touching the mouse — fast, but easy to fire once too many times and start editing on the wrong sheet without noticing the tab changed.
Instantly scrolls back to and re-selects the active cell, no matter how far you've scrolled away — the fastest way back to where you actually are.

Opens Go To, and "Special..." from there lets you select every blank cell, every formula, every constant, or every conditional-format cell in the sheet at once — genuinely powerful for auditing, and a live minefield if you then hit Delete on that selection.

Opens Paste Special — paste values only, formats only, transpose, or paste-link. The most consequential choice most people never make deliberately: pasting normally over formulas silently replaces them with whatever was on the clipboard.

cmd: Paste Special → Link   ·   Mac: Paste Special → Link
desc: Creates a live formula reference back to the source cell instead of copying a static value — looks identical to a normal paste in the cell, but the pasted value now changes whenever the ORIGINAL cell changes, even in a different sheet or workbook.

cmd: Ctrl+Alt+V then E (Transpose)   ·   Mac: Cmd+Ctrl+V then Transpose
desc: Flips a copied row into a column (or vice versa) on paste — a genuine power move, and a common source of misaligned data when the source range wasn't exactly what you thought it was.

Legacy array-formula entry (CSE formula) — the formula behaves differently from a normal one and is genuinely hard to spot later (it just shows curly braces in the formula bar). Modern Excel mostly auto-handles this via dynamic arrays, but files built in older Excel are full of these.
Opens the VBA editor. Pressing F5 in there runs whatever macro is currently selected immediately — no confirmation, and macros can do literally anything the Excel process can do on your machine.

Saves in place, overwriting the existing file with no version history unless AutoSave/version control is on — the shortcut people fire on reflex right before realizing they just overwrote the last good copy of a shared template.
Creates named ranges from selected row/column labels in one step — genuinely useful, and it silently creates workbook-scoped names that can collide with names used elsewhere in a large model.
